name: Throat singing practice

lead: Throat singing is a family of traditional vocal styles from Mongolia, Tuva and Tibet. Some voice-training circles practise low styles hoping for a deeper voice.
No studies have tested whether this changes ordinary speech.

paras: Singers shape the mouth and throat so particular harmonics are amplified, and some styles use the false vocal folds as a second sound source.
Sources reviewed report no health data on the practice; voice clinicians generally discuss strain as a concern with any forced vocal technique.

lead: Throat singing practice, in looksmaxxing and voice-training discussion, refers to using overtone or throat-singing techniques, such as Tuvan kargyraa or Tibetan chant, to train a lower or more resonant voice. Overtone singing is a traditional vocal technique in which a singer shapes the vocal tract so that selected harmonics stand out, producing two audible pitches at once.[1]

The techniques come from Mongolia, Tuva and Tibet, and Western musicians took them up from the 1960s.[1] Some styles add a second sound source from the false vocal folds.[1] No study was found testing whether practising throat singing changes everyday speaking pitch; the Wikipedia article notes acoustic and MRI studies of the technique but reports nothing about voice health effects.[1]

paras: Mongolia's main style is khoomii; Tuvan styles include khoomei, sygyt and kargyraa; Tibetan Buddhist chanting includes very low-pitched styles used by monks.[1] UNESCO recognised Sardinian cantu a tenore in 2005, and composers such as Stockhausen incorporated overtone singing in the late 1960s.[1]

Voice-training communities discuss low-register styles as a way to practise vocal tract control and a deeper tone. The sources reviewed give no evidence on whether this alters habitual speaking pitch, or on any strain risk.

timeline.event: Stockhausen composes Stimmung using overtone singing.[1]
UNESCO recognises Sardinian cantu a tenore as intangible heritage.[1]
